blocks.value: **If a derived class defines a method with the same name, the same number and types of parameters, and the same return type as a method in the base class, the definition in the derived class is said to override the definition in the base class.**

Writing `@Override` above a method asks the compiler to verify that it really does override something. If you misspell the name or get a parameter type wrong, you get an error instead of a method that silently never runs. It is optional, and worth using every time.
**Overriding is not overloading.** They sound alike and are unrelated:

rows: At **run time**, by the object's actual class

blocks.value: To forbid overriding, mark a method `final`. A subclass that tries to override a `final` method fails to compile. A whole class can be `final` as well, in which case it cannot be extended at all. `String` is a `final` class.
